passages.label: A
passages.text: Think about why the neighbours want to celebrate before choosing the venue, and an activity might bring families together, raise money or share something about local history. The UK government guide encourages people to find advice that fits their event, and a group can make better choices about space, food and information once it knows who will take part.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The initial plan should match the size and purpose of the event, and a group may want to celebrate a local history, share traditional food or introduce families to part of their culture. These aims lead to different choices, and a food event needs suitable food-safety advice, and a street event may need permission from the local authority. Organisers also need to consider first aid, toilets, access and the route people will use. The guide advises organisers to find guidance that fits their particular event.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Planning also includes the people who will take part, and a visitor needs to know where an event is, when it starts and how to get help. Clear signs can help, especially at a large or popular event. Volunteers can welcome people, answer simple questions and tell an organiser if a problem develops, and they should know who makes important decisions. A volunteer does not need to solve every difficulty alone, and the plan should make clear when to ask for help. A group can ask a visitor afterwards whether the place and the main activities were easy to find.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The site and number of guests affect the arrangements. While a small group can have a party indoors, people gathering to have a celebration in a public place may need space for spectators and emergency access. A parade needs a route. Volunteers may decorate a hall and arrange entertainment, and anyone serving a dish should know where to take care of waste or put equipment after use. Give guests a contact person if they have a problem, and a plan helps an event take place safely while visitors can have fun and local routines continue.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A small gift can be a treat for the lucky winner of a game, while a shared meal may be the highlight of a different event. Fireworks are one possible activity at a celebration, and an organiser can also choose music, a story or a chance for every visitor to try something. After it is over, ask people which parts helped them join in. Their answers can show how to make the next event easier to understand and welcoming for more neighbours. A festival can attract people from outside the neighbourhood, so someone who plans to go to an event needs information about its finishing time and transport.

R_H2.passageTitle: Day of the Dead: Memory and Meaning

passages.label: A
passages.text: In indigenous communities of Mexico, Día de los Muertos remembers the temporary return of deceased relatives and loved ones. UNESCO says these observances take place from the end of October to the beginning of November. This time also marks the end of the yearly maize-growing cycle. And the occasion is not simply a public show. It is a way for families and communities to remember people who have died and to share an important part of their culture. And this gives the days a meaning that is both personal and communal.

passages.label: B
passages.text: Before the festival, families may decorate a home or a grave. A dish that a relative used to enjoy can be set out, and a child may take care of flowers beside it. People who go to a festival as spectators sometimes look for a parade or entertainment. A family preparing to have a celebration may focus on remembrance, including the significance of preparing an offering together.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Flowers are a visible highlight of many ofrendas. A Mexican government source explains that cempasúchil is used to decorate homes, altars, offerings and cemeteries. Its yellow or orange colour has long been linked with the sun. Some people believe that its strong smell can guide the dead towards an offering. This belief should not be presented as a scientific fact. It is part of the meaning people give to the flower. Different families and communities may use their own traditional choices and arrangements.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The festival has a long history. UNESCO explains that it brings together pre-Hispanic religious rites and Catholic feasts introduced by Europeans in the sixteenth century. The annual meeting of the living and the dead can affirm an individual’s place in society and strengthen indigenous communities. People may take part by preparing food, visiting a cemetery, arranging an altar or sharing family stories. A visitor can learn from these practices, but should remember that they have meaning within communities, not only as colourful images.

passages.label: E
passages.text: People celebrate in different ways, and a visitor lucky enough to be invited to a family meal can learn directly from those taking part. Someone who associates popular festivals with fireworks may first look for a public activity. The families described in these accounts make preparation, food and memory the centre of their days. A gift on an offering can recall a particular person. Look at what has been placed there and ask whose memory is being honoured. That question helps the visitor understand why the occasion continues to matter. Public events can attract interest in the tradition. A costume can make a parade visually distinctive, while a museum lecture might explain regional differences and the commemorative meaning of a family gathering.

passages.label: A
passages.text: A visitor may be lucky enough to see fireworks or hear music on a festival night in Oman. A museum can help the visitor learn something about the history and skills behind what people celebrate. The National Museum's Intangible Heritage Gallery presents traditions that people practise and pass on, and it gives visitors a way to ask how a piece of music or a skill can reach the next generation.

passages.label: B
passages.text: The gallery turns this question into a learning activity, and it displays musical instruments, and interactive screens help a visitor find out about instruments and types of traditional Omani music. The screens also let people listen to songs by notable performers. Another section introduces dance genres through descriptions and video links, and these displays cannot replace learning directly from a performer, but they can give young people and travellers a starting point. They show that listening and watching carefully are useful ways to take part in cultural learning.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Craft skills are also part of this story. Oman’s Ministry of Heritage and Tourism describes craft heritage as knowledge, skills and techniques passed down through generations, as well as the products people make. Its examples include work with wood, silver, leather, pottery, palm fronds and fabric, and a traditional object may be useful, beautiful or both. For example, a craftsperson’s work can connect materials, tools and local experience, and the important highlight is not simply the finished item. It is also the skill and care needed to make it.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The museum can attract people who usually go to an event for entertainment. Someone who plans to have a party or have a celebration may notice a costume on display or ask how to make a dish. The museum can also hold a lecture. Learning about the original setting helps people enjoy the object and see why staff take care of it.

passages.label: E
passages.text: A small gift made by a craftsperson is more than an object to put on a shelf. A visitor can ask about the materials and watch how a detail is made. A museum may give this learning activity a starting point, while demonstration and training can keep the skill in use. That is one way people take part in a living culture and respect those who teach it. A popular display can therefore lead to a longer interest in the skills behind the finished work. A public festival or a parade may take place outside the museum. Families may have fun there while seeing how people decorate items of daily use.

questions.prompt: What can a visitor do with the screens that goes beyond seeing instruments in a case?
options: See the objects without being offered a way to hear the music.
Take instruments out of their cases without supervision.
Explore types of instruments and listen to songs associated with the tradition.

questions.prompt: Why can a well-made object by itself give an incomplete account of a craft?
options: The heritage is concerned only with the price people paid for the object.

It has to be used at a public festival for the maker’s skills to matter.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–C, for each question.
questions.prompt: What makes local experience relevant when a craftsperson works with a material?
options: It means every worker can make the object without tools.

Checking only the size of the completed object.

questions.prompt: To understand what goes from a skilled person to a learner, how should a visitor use the exhibits?
